clinicalPearls: Chilblain lupus erythematosus is a chronic form of cutaneous lupus in which cold-induced, tender violaceous papules and plaques develop on acral sites such as fingers, toes, ears, nose and heels.
It should not be confused with sarcoidosis-related lupus pernio, a quite different entity affecting the central face; chilblain lupus is a lupus-specific dermatosis provoked by cold and damp.
Lesions resemble idiopathic chilblains but are more persistent, may ulcerate or become hyperkeratotic and fissured, and do not resolve promptly with warming alone.
A proportion of patients meet criteria for or later develop systemic lupus erythematosus, so systemic assessment and long-term monitoring are important.
A rare familial form of chilblain lupus is caused by mutations in TREX1 or SAMHD1 and belongs to the type I interferonopathy spectrum, overlapping with Aicardi-Goutieres syndrome.

Histology shows an interface dermatitis with a superficial and deep perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate, and direct immunofluorescence often demonstrates lupus-band deposition at the dermoepidermal junction.
Management centres on cold avoidance, warm clothing and smoking cessation, with topical or systemic corticosteroids, antimalarials and calcium-channel blockers used for persistent disease.
Distinguishing chilblain lupus from ordinary perniosis rests on chronicity, acral photodistribution, histopathology, immunofluorescence and lupus serology.
reference.pathophysiology: Chilblain lupus is a cold-triggered variant of chronic cutaneous lupus erythematosus in which low temperature and microvascular vasoconstriction combine with a lupus-specific inflammatory response. Cold-induced hypoperfusion of acral skin, together with an interface dermatitis driven by autoreactive T lymphocytes and a type I interferon signature, produces the characteristic tender violaceous lesions. Immune complex deposition and complement activation at the dermoepidermal junction contribute to tissue injury, and impaired clearance of nucleic acids underlies the familial monogenic forms associated with TREX1 and SAMHD1 mutations, which drive chronic interferon overproduction. The acral, cold-exposed distribution reflects the additive effect of vasospastic hypoxia and photo- and cold-provoked immunological activity on skin already predisposed by the lupus diathesis.
additionalDifferentials: Systemic lupus erythematosus with acral involvement
Sarcoidosis (true lupus pernio of the face)
Raynaud phenomenon and other vasospastic disorders
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy for histopathology showing interface dermatitis with deep perivascular infiltrate
Direct immunofluorescence for a lupus band at the dermoepidermal junction
Antinuclear antibody and extractable nuclear antigen panel
Complement levels and anti-dsDNA antibodies to assess systemic activity
Cryoglobulins and cold agglutinins to exclude cold-precipitable proteins
Genetic testing for TREX1/SAMHD1 in familial or early-onset cases
redFlags: Features suggesting evolution to systemic lupus such as arthritis, nephritis or cytopenias
Ulceration or necrosis of acral lesions
Family history or early childhood onset suggesting a monogenic interferonopathy
Systemic symptoms including fever, weight loss or serositis
Laboratory evidence of active systemic disease (low complement, high anti-dsDNA)
reference.prognosis: Chilblain lupus tends to run a chronic, relapsing course closely linked to cold exposure and may persist for years; a minority progress to systemic lupus erythematosus, so periodic reassessment is warranted.
pitfalls: Confusing chilblain lupus with the facial sarcoidal lupus pernio, an unrelated condition
Dismissing persistent acral lesions as ordinary chilblains and missing the lupus diagnosis
Failing to screen for systemic lupus at diagnosis and during follow-up
Overlooking a familial interferonopathy in early-onset or familial cases
Attributing lesions solely to cold and neglecting biopsy and serology
references: Dubois' Lupus Erythematosus and Related Syndromes
management: Cold and damp avoidance with insulation of the extremities and smoking cessation form the essential first-line measure
Topical corticosteroids or calcineurin inhibitors for individual acral lesions
Antimalarials such as hydroxychloroquine are the mainstay systemic therapy, with a calcium-channel blocker such as nifedipine added for the vasospastic component
Escalate refractory disease to systemic immunomodulation, with JAK inhibitors particularly relevant in TREX1/SAMHD1-related interferonopathy forms
Monitor for evolution into systemic lupus erythematosus with periodic review and complement, anti-dsDNA and autoantibody testing
Offer genetic counselling and consider TREX1/SAMHD1 testing in familial chilblain lupus within the type I interferonopathy spectrum
